paragraphs.text: Majority of young people support more hands-on learning from age 14.

Teenagers have thrown their support behind a shake-up to vocational learning as the government steps up efforts to tackle youth unemployment and challenge outdated attitudes towards technical education.

The majority of young people (84%) overwhelmingly support new options for 14-year-olds that combine practical technical learning (such as coding, construction or manufacturing) with core academic subjects (such as English and Maths) - an ambition announced by the Prime Minister in his first week in office and now being delivered on.
Two weeks ago, the government unveiled plans for Vocational GCSEs - a fundamental change to the education system to put hands-on education on an equal footing with academic from 14.

This shake-up builds on the reforms to introduce rigorous new V Levels which will be available from September 2027 to provide high-quality vocational training for 16 to 19-year-olds. They will sit alongside A Levels and T Levels, and will be equivalent to one A Level, allowing students to mix and match academic and vocational subjects if they are unsure where to specialise.
With nearly a million young people aged 16 to 24 currently out of education, employment or training, the government is determined to ensure the system works for every young person.
Vocational GCSEs will have nationally set standards, unlike the existing Technical Awards, and grading and assessment will be regulated by Ofqual to ensure full parity with traditional GCSEs.
Of those 500 polled, who are due to or have recently made choices about their options at aged 14 and 16:
Nearly half (44%) say vocational and technical routes are looked down on by their peers.
Over a third (37%) feel pressure from their parents to choose academic options from aged 16.
When thinking about their future, their biggest concern was ending up in a job they do not enjoy (69%).
Nearly half (46%) are concerned that advances in artificial intelligence could reduce employment opportunities.
More than half (52%) said they worry about having the right skills for the jobs of the future.

Vocational GCSEs will sit alongside traditional GCSEs and will eventually replace the current Technical Awards. They are set to be available in some subjects as early as September 2029, as part of broader new technical pathways starting in September 2028. English, Maths and Science will remain a common entitlement.

Subject options could include Business Management and Finance, Creative Media Production, Digital Tech, Child Development, and Building and Construction, supporting progression into further study through T Levels and V Levels in these subjects, or through A Levels.
A consultation to shape Vocational GCSEs will be published before the end of the year.
From September 2027, the first V Levels will be available in Education and Early Years, Finance and Accounting, and Digital which could lead into university or an apprenticeship.
For those who need support to pass English and Maths before progressing there will be two new qualifications also available from September 2027:
Foundation Certificates will provide a one-year bridging route before progressing to V Levels, T Levels or A Levels, initially in Education and Early Years and Digital.

A separate two-year pathway through an Occupational Certificate will be available for those who want to go directly into work or an apprenticeship, with initial subjects in Catering and Hospitality and Education and Early Years.
